chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
title: Why the army was wrong for Lester; Collins slipping away from training
summary: Collins says regimentation and uncomprehending officers could destroy Prez, and describes dodging maneuvers until a master sergeant moved him into the band.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x:
Well, in the first place regimentation, you know, he couldn't go for that at all. This I knew. And he -- Lester was a very -- he was an introvert in a lot of ways, and a lot of people just wouldn't understand Lester. You know, they wouldn't understand him, and wouldn't know how to deal with him. Square. When I say a square I mean someone naturally out of the music business, wouldn't understand him. And they could -- and they could destroy a person, you know, like with me. When I went in the army and I had to go through all this training and all of this, which I had never done anything like this in my life. And I would slip off in the morning before they all went to the -- to do maneuvers, and you know, take this training. I could go to the band barracks and go to sleep.

So I did an awful lot of extra duty for doing this. They used to really punish me and I'd have to walk with full field packs and all this. But I just wasn't cut out for this. So finally the band -- it was-- we had a sergeant major in there, master sergeant, rather, by the name of Barry Ellis. He prevailed upon the colonel to just transfer me to the band. So I went into the band. So we stayed there for quite a while, and towards the last part of my army stay I went to Oakland, California, and they put me into a port company.
